title: Before asking AI to code your trading bot, ask it to find the decisions you haven’t made
author: Electrical_Waltz_888
selftext:
“Buy when price breaks resistance, put a stop below support and take profit at twice the risk.”

That sounds reasonably clear—until you try to automate it.

Which resistance level? Does an intraday move count, or must a candle close above it? If the entry order only partially fills, what quantity should the stop protect?

AI can produce code without asking those questions. The code may run while making decisions you never consciously chose.

Here’s a prompt you can try before asking for code:

“Review this proposed trading rule: \[paste your rule\].

1. Quote every term that needs a measurable definition.
2. List missing decisions about signal timing, entry, exits, position size and order handling.
3. Mark decisions I haven’t made UNRESOLVED.
4. Mark interpretations you introduce ASSUMPTION.
5. Walk through a partial fill, missing price data and an order timeout. Explain what my current rules specify and where they are silent.

Do not choose settings, recommend trades or write code yet. Ask me to resolve the gaps.”

For example, “retry if the order times out” hides an important question: did the broker reject the order, or accept it without returning confirmation? Retrying without checking could create a duplicate position.

The useful output is a list of decisions to resolve—not proof that the strategy works. You still need to verify broker behaviour, test the implementation and examine results after realistic costs. AI can miss gaps too.

What instruction sounded clear when you wrote it but became ambiguous when you tried to automate it?

Disclosure: I’m the author of" The Complete Guide to AI Powered Trading". The book develops this approach through worked examples and includes 50 reusable prompts covering learning, planning, specification building and review.

Book: [https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HNM97TQ9)

comments.author: Tradenoss
comments.body: "close everything at the end of the day" is a good one to test this on. end of which session, what if the market closes early, what if the exit order doesn't fill before the close. sounds obvious until you write it down

replies.author: Electrical_Waltz_888
replies.body:
Exactly. “Submit an exit order” and “confirm the position is flat” are two different conditions.
The rule needs an exchange calendar, a cutoff relative to the actual session close, and a defined response if the exit is rejected or only partially filled. If the position remains open, that’s an exception requiring escalation—not a completed end-of-day exit.
I’d test an early close alongside a cancellation race: the exit looks unfilled, the system retries, then the original fill confirmation arrives. Without checking order status first, an attempt to flatten can create a reverse position.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the candle-close vs intraday-touch choice alone can flip a backtest, since a touch rule fills on wicks a close rule never sees. and most backtests skip the partial fill question by pretending everything fills.

I made Quantradin for the step after that prompt: the rule you wrote in words gets tested only on bars that had already closed, then trades fake dollars on live quotes, so the gaps you never decided show up before real money does.

quantradin.com

did the prompt ever flag something you'd already coded around without noticing?

replies.author: Electrical_Waltz_888
replies.body:
The key issue is whether the engine exposes missing decisions or quietly supplies its own.
Closed-bar evaluation addresses signal timing. It doesn’t resolve execution assumptions. A paper fill on a live quote still needs a model for available quantity, partial fills and slippage.
If cancellation behaviour is undefined, does Quantradin flag it as unresolved or choose a default? And when an order partially fills, how does it handle protection of the filled quantity while the remainder stays open?
Those are the details I’d examine before treating paper results as evidence that the implementation matches the intended rules.
